big: Two funds can both be called multi-asset and be taxed differently. One rule sets what a multi-asset fund must hold. A second rule, about equity, sets the tax. Learn both before you say a word about tax.

lines: My bank manager says multi-asset funds are taxed like equity funds. Is that true for every one?
Not every one. The tax class depends on how much equity the fund holds, and arbitrage counts as equity here. Let us see how the rules sit.

rows.name: The floor: 10% in each of three

alt: Three bars: the minimum mix, a common mix, and a mix that fails the rule
caps: SEBI's rule: a multi-asset allocation fund holds at least 10% in each of at least three asset classes.
That is only the floor. The striped part is the manager's choice.
A common mix is equity, debt and gold or silver, sometimes with REITs and InvITs.
Equity and debt alone fail the rule. Without a third class at 10% or more, it is a different category.

alt: Three funds with equity plus arbitrage weights of 70, 50 and 65 percent
caps: Tax follows equity, and arbitrage counts as equity. Fund A: 35% equity plus 35% arbitrage is 70%.
At 65% or more it is taxed like an equity fund. Long-term gains count after 12 months.
Fund B has 50% equity. Between 35% and 65%, gains turn long-term only after 24 months.
Fund C: 40% plus 25% is exactly 65%, so equity tax. Add up each fund's structure, not its name.

h: The same gain, two tax classes
rows: Tax on ₹2 lakh gain at 18 months, ₹ thousand
alt: Two bars comparing tax on a gain sold at 18 months
caps: Same gain of ₹2,00,000, sold after 18 months by a client in the 30% slab.
Equity-taxed fund: it is long-term, so 12.5%. About ₹25,000.
Fund with 50% equity: 18 months is under 24, so it is short-term and taxed at slab. About ₹60,000.
Before cess and the yearly ₹1.25 lakh equity exemption. Waiting six more months would change class B.

q: A fund house proposes a multi-asset fund with 55% equity and 45% debt, and no gold or other third asset. Can it carry the multi-asset allocation label?
opts: Yes, because the mix adds up to 100% and equity and debt are the two main asset classes
No. The rule needs at least 10% in each of three classes, and this mix has only two
Yes, if the debt part is split between government bonds and corporate bonds
No, because every multi-asset fund must hold at least 40% in gold or silver
why: Adding to 100% is not the test. The rule asks for three classes each at 10% or more, which this mix lacks.
With only equity and debt there is no third class at 10% or more, so it does not meet the multi-asset allocation rule.
Government and corporate bonds are both debt. Splitting one class in two does not make a new asset class.
The rule sets 10% as the floor for each of three classes. It does not ask for 40% in gold or silver.

q: A multi-asset fund holds 30% equity, 35% arbitrage, 20% debt and 15% gold. A client says it cannot be equity-taxed, as only 30% is real equity. What is correct?
opts: It is not equity-taxed, because only the 30% in directional equity counts here
It is taxed like debt, because debt and gold together make up 35% of the fund
It is taxed at slab rate in every case, because it also holds gold in the portfolio
It is equity-taxed: equity plus arbitrage makes 65%, which reaches the line
why: For the tax test, arbitrage positions count as equity, so the 30% figure alone is the wrong number to use.
Debt and gold at 35% do not make it a debt fund. The test looks at equity, including arbitrage, at 65%.
Holding gold does not decide the class. Equity share, including arbitrage, decides it.
For the tax test, arbitrage counts with equity. 30% plus 35% is 65%, so the fund is taxed like an equity fund.

q: A client in the 30% slab sells after 18 months with a ₹2 lakh gain. One fund is equity-taxed, the other has 50% equity. How much more tax does the second one cost, before cess and exemption?
opts: About ₹35,000 more: 12.5% on one gain, the 30% slab on the other
About ₹17,500 more, because only a gap of five percentage points counts here
About ₹60,000 more, because the second fund's whole tax bill is the extra cost
About ₹25,000 more, because the equity fund's own tax bill is the extra cost
why: 12.5% of ₹2 lakh is ₹25,000. 30% of ₹2 lakh is ₹60,000. The difference is ₹35,000 (17.5 percentage points).
The gap between 12.5% and 30% is 17.5 points, not five. On ₹2 lakh that is ₹35,000.
₹60,000 is the full tax on the second fund. The first fund also pays ₹25,000, so the extra is less.
₹25,000 is what the equity-taxed fund pays. It is one of the two bills, not the gap between them.

q: The 50%-equity fund holds a ₹2 lakh gain at 18 months. The client has no urgent need and asks about waiting. What should the adviser say?
opts: Sell now, because the gain is taxed at the same rate at 18 months or at 24 months
Switch to another fund first, since a switch is not a sale and so no tax applies to it
Six more months moves the gain to 12.5%; weigh that against the need for money
Always wait, because a tax saving is more certain than anything the market can do
why: The rate differs. Under 24 months this class is taxed at slab, and after that at 12.5%.
A switch is a redemption and a fresh purchase, so it triggers tax and restarts the holding period.
At 24 months the gain turns long-term at 12.5%. It is a trade-off with market risk and the client's needs, not a rule.
Waiting leaves the client exposed to market moves meanwhile. The tax saving is one factor among several.

pts: A multi-asset fund holds at least 10% in each of at least three asset classes, usually equity, debt and gold or silver.
Equity plus arbitrage at 65% or more means equity tax, long-term after 12 months. At 35% to 65%, long-term starts after 24 months.
Add up each fund's actual mix before you speak about tax. Names do not decide the class.
